output.title: Designing against positioning drift starts with one anchor
output.body:
If you want to design against positioning drift, keep it to one bounded workflow decision: what is the one customer problem or outcome your business says it reliably solves? That anchor is the filter. Everything else should be checked against it.

For a small business, the practical question is not whether you can write nicer copy. It is whether your current workflow keeps sending mixed signals. Pick one repeatable place where drift shows up: how you triage customer inquiries, how you answer sales questions, or how you negotiate project scope. Choose the one that most often creates confusion and make it visible.

Then write the anchor in plain English and use it as a manual check for a short period. If the same questions keep coming up, or if scope keeps expanding in ways that pull you off-message, you have found a real control point. If the workflow stays consistent, the anchor is probably doing its job. Boring, in the good way.

AI can help later by enforcing that wording inside documents, email, CRM, or back-office workflows, but only after the owner has confirmed the anchor is actually right. Bareni’s current AI work is still limited to self-built demos and workflow design; that is not the same as a customer-validated system. The decision still belongs to you; automation is for consistency, not authority.

Which workflow in your business surfaces positioning ambiguity most often? Start there and test the anchor first.
